summary: Our team, Above Average Intelligence, wanted to find a place on Earth where astronauts and rovers could practice for the Moon base area near the lunar South Pole. We picked the Rawlinson Range in Western Australia as a stand-in for Malapert Massif, one of NASA’s 13 Artemis III candidate regions. Using NASA’s SRTM 30 m elevation data, we measured the slope of every pixel and kept only ground with at least 50 m of relief, since flat plains aren’t useful for training. That cut flat terrain from 86.6% to 10.1%. Four of the five slope bands landed near the estimates for Malapert, but the 10-20 degree band ran high at 45.3%. So the profile is broadly consistent, but it’s not a proven match, and the Malapert numbers are only preliminary estimates. Rawlinson can’t copy the Moon’s gravity, extreme cold, sharp dust, or lack of air, so those need separate tests. What it can help with is climbing practice, rover path planning, and navigating without GPS. Our next step is to check our numbers against real LOLA slope data from NASA.
details:
Our project looks for a place on Earth whose terrain shape is similar to Malapert Massif, a mountain near the lunar South Pole that is one of NASA's 13 Artemis III candidate regions. Our case study is the Rawlinson Range in Western Australia. We took NASA's SRTM 30 m elevation data, calculated the slope of every pixel, and kept only ground with at least 50 m of local relief so flat plains did not count. We then compared five slope bands with preliminary Malapert estimates. Flat terrain dropped from 86.6% to 10.1%, and four of the five bands landed in or near the lunar estimates. The 10 to 20 degree band ran high at 45.3%, so we describe the result as broadly consistent, not a proven match.

The site could be used for astronaut climbing and footing practice, rover path planning and tipping risk tests, practicing the traverse from a landing zone to a destination, drone hazard detection, and navigating without GPS. It is remote and not a standard NASA training site, and the same method can be repeated on other candidate sites.

We used NASA's SRTM 1 arc-second elevation data, and we plan to check our results against LRO LOLA slope data next. We presented the project as an interactive slide deck with clickable chapters and click-to-reveal challenges.

Instead of just choosing a place that looks Moon-like, we measured the terrain shape with numbers and filtered out flat ground. We also state clearly what the site cannot do.

We considered several limits. SRTM at 30 m smooths steep features, the Malapert figures are estimates and not LOLA-derived, and 100 m and 150 m relief cutoffs give much steeper profiles. Only about 10% of our study area is high-relief terrain. Gravity, extreme cold, sharp glassy dust, lighting, and the lack of air do not match, so each needs separate testing. The site is remote, on Aboriginal-held land, so we would engage the land holders first, and it has summer heat above 40°C plus snakes, insects, and spinifex. Our next steps are to check against real LOLA data, measure the usable area and how connected it is, and test gravity offload, suits, and regolith simulant.

projectRefs: We used Google Earth Engine with a free 30-metre elevation map of Earth. The code calculates how steep every pixel is and sorts it into five bands. Because the area around the range is mostly flat desert, it also measures local relief and keeps only the hilly ground. It then counts how much of that falls into each band. That gave us the percentages on the slide, and the same method can be run on lunar data. This code was generated by SI.
